speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: If our economy stagnates, it will dampen aspirations and hopes for a better future and may lead to unease and insecurity among our people.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The inherent constraints facing us – land, labour and carbon – will become more acute.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: We have also got to content with a more fractured and contested world, with greater willingness of countries to use economic leverage to exert their interests.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: There are also profound shifts in the economic landscape.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The rapid rise of new disruptive technologies such as generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) and the wider adoptions of big data analytics, cloud computing, e-commerce and automation technologies present both challenges and opportunities to Singapore.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: All these may sound daunting but fortunately, we are able to respond from a position of strength.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: So, how do we grow the economy going forward?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Allow me to just touch on three areas.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Having state of the art companies' hub and base here helps overcome our scale limitations and enable the proliferations of technologies and the development of skilled talents here.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: To achieve that, we must tick the boxes in the list of checklist that investors look for.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Among the key requirements are excellent infrastructure and connectivity, diverse talent pool, trusted and innovative hub, strong financial standing and political stability.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: And that is why we must keep working on enhancing our overall propositions; continue to invest heavily into our workforce, in infrastructure and also innovation; as well enhancing our connectivity, our economic fundamentals; and to have sound and consistent policies.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The Ministry of Trade and Industry (MTI) has in earlier Budget Committees of Supply (COS) outlined our manufacturing and services strategies.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Although manufacturing now accounts for less than 30% of our gross domestic product (GDP), it remains a very important pillar in our economy.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Singapore is the eighth largest exporter of high-tech goods in the world and home to many high-value industries like precision engineering, MedTech, aerospace, semiconductors and so on.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Besides the jobs and value-add that it creates, the manufacturing sector helps add further resilience to our economy and also helps contribute to the growth in the services sectors.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Other than attracting and anchoring frontiers global manufacturers to base here, we should also keep working on developing and growing the manufacturing capabilities of our local enterprises, with the aim grow them into regional champions in their own right.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Our services sector covers a wide spectrum of businesses, including both outward-oriented sectors like financial services, logistics, trade as well as domestic-facing ones like food and beverages (F&B) and retail trade.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: At last year's MTI COS, Minister Gan shared that our Services 2030 vision seeks to harness the growth opportunities in the areas of digitalisation and sustainability and to anchor Singapore as a leading, vibrant hub for businesses, lifestyle and tourism.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: This strategy and the focuses would play to our strengths and minimise our shortcomings.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: To continue to be the service hub of choice for global businesses, we need to make our city the among the most business-friendly and among the most liveable city in the world.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Hence, the longer-term urban planning such as the Masterplan by the Urban Redevelopment Authority (URA) and the infrastructure upgrades in transport, recreational facilities, healthcare, convention facilities and so on – all adds to making us a conducive hub to offer services to the consumers and businesses of the world.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Thirdly, we grow our economy by continually investing in new technologies and capabilities.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Last year, we saw the rapid emergence of AI powered applications and systems, and the momentum is likely to continue and increase this year.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: We need to develop homegrown AI technologies, grow the AI talent pool and encourage adoption of AI technologies among enterprises.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Besides AI, we would also need to sustain our investment in research and innovations to deepen our scientific capabilities and bolster the startup ecosystem here to capture value.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Fifth, in the Deputy Prime Minister's Budget Statement and in his round-up speech as well, he mentioned about developing local pipeline of corporate leadership talent and more support to help Singaporeans gain overseas experience.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Can I ask for more details of this plan?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: So, can I seek an update on our tourism revitalisation effort?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: What more can we do to ensure that Singapore remains an attractive tourist destination amidst the intense global and regional competition?

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The rise in manpower costs is a major concern.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: This, combined with the increased costs of raw materials, rents, utilities and other operational expenses is exerting immense pressure on their already thin margins.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The heightened interest rates environment also adds further pressure on financing costs, adding challenges to SMEs' access to capital for growth and innovation.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The need for digital transformation has shifted from being a luxury to a necessity for survival and growth.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Another pressing issue is the environmental impact and the increasing demand for green compliance.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Many SMEs lack the knowledge and resources to transform towards greener practices, even as they face increasing pressure from counterparts and regulations requiring adherence to green standards.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: This gap further hinders their ability to compete effectively and sustainably.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: But the most significant support measures are those tilted towards firms that can restructure and transform.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Therefore, to support SMEs to embark on this transformation journey, I would like to ask the Government to double down on three fronts.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: First, we must strongly promote collaborations between larger companies and SMEs in the area of supplier development and co-creation.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: This inclusion – to include SMEs in the application – should be particularly emphasised for high-value investments such as research and development (R&D) and innovation related grants.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: By doing so, it will not only incentivise large entities to collaborate with SMEs, but also ensure the benefits of such Government-backed programmes extend across the broader business ecosystem.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: This arrangement should enable banks to take on more risk and provide more favourable terms to our SMEs.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: By offering this level of support, the Government is really in a good position to expect participating financial institutions to improve loan conditions for our SMEs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Mr Chairman, Singapore has been bracing itself for a period of slow growth and high inflation as Deputy Prime Minister Heng Swee Keat has pointed out in his Budget Speech this year.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Our population is rapidly ageing, our local workforce growth will eventually slow down to zero.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: An ageing population will lead to increase in social spending, decreased consumption and decreased labour output.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: There are also constraints of land, power and carbon.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: How will our GDP look like over the next decade?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We must not let this happen to Singapore.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I have three suggestions for the Ministry to consider.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: First, we must increase the amount of capital and adoption of innovation and technology by our SMEs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Singapore is already amongst the world's leaders in automation, especially in industrial robots.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It was just behind South Korea in 2021.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: For our growth to continue, we need to intensify automation and innovation in our SMEs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: What is the current progress and plans to intensify capital investment and adoption of innovation by SMEs?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Next, we need to have more of our companies operating abroad to bring in income and job opportunities.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Economically, we need to focus on our gross national income (GNI) per capita as much as GDP per capita.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Singapore is fortunate to be in Southeast Asia, one of the fastest growing regions in the world.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: With a young and still-growing population of 650 million, Singapore can have access to a large market and pool of talent.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Our companies must seize the limited window to expand in the region.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: How has MTI helped our Singapore companies to expand in the region?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: What are the future plans to help SMEs go regional?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Lastly, we must seize the opportunity provided by AI for Singapore to continue to punch above our weight.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: AI has the potential to improve our workers' productivity tremendously.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Yet, AI will require significant resources, especially power and talent, for R&D.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: How is the Ministry ensuring that Singapore has the requisite infrastructure and talent for companies to keep pace and deepen AI work?

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Chairman, in an era where global economies are increasingly interconnected and digital technologies are rapidly evolving, the need for our businesses to stay competitive has never been more critical.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: As we navigate through the complexities of the 21st century – including the pressing challenges posed by climate change – the imperative for digital innovation, global market expansion and sustainable practices is paramount to not only surviving but thrive in the global marketplace.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Digitalisation and sustainable practices are essential pillars for resilience and growth in the complex web of global supply chains and commerce.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Digitalisation by enabling seamless integration of technologies, facilitates unparalleled efficiencies, agility and connectivity among businesses worldwide, thereby enhancing competitiveness and access to markets.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Concurrently, sustainability practices address the urgent need to minimise environmental impact and promote responsibility sourcing and production methods.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: As such, what are some of the key measures that MTI is undertaking to support our sectors and firms in their transformation efforts, particularly in digitalisation, internationalisation and sustainability?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Several countries have implemented various policies, including new tax incentives and credits, enhanced investment allowances, targeted sectoral support and direct subsidies to individual companies.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: This land scarce little red dot, with no domestic market to speak of, where wages and living costs are higher than in many other jurisdictions.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: We cannot be complacent and a competitive tax regime is critical.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: It directly alleviates the tax burden for businesses while allowing EDB and Enterprise Singapore to target the companies and sectors that will best contribute to economic growth; as well as opportunities and jobs for our people and our local enterprises.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: A good understanding of how the scheme will be implemented and its potential benefits for the Singapore economy and Singaporeans is therefore helpful for both businesses and the public.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: To that end, I have a few questions for the Minister.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Two, the list of economic activities and qualifying expenditures appear to be quite broad; can the Minister give more specifics on the sectors and qualifying expenditures that can be expected?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Three, how can we ensure that the tax credit will incentivise capital investment and drive desired outcomes, such as higher productivity or decarbonisation targets; and help MNEs achieve those targets?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: And lastly, how else is the Government supporting businesses to stay competitive?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Ms Jessica Tan, please take your two cuts together.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: With geopolitical uncertainties, rapid technology development, structural disruptions and inflationary pressures, Budget 2024 signals the urgency for businesses to transform.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: It is no longer a good-to-do but a must-do if businesses want to stay relevant, continue to do business and grow.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Business transformation is not easy as it involves business process and operational changes; the adoption of relevant digital technology; as well as the need to build new and deep capabilities of employees to address the structural disruptions.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: With climate change, we see increasing legislation of sustainability standards and disclosures.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This will require that companies commit to and transition to sustainable ways of doing business, if they want to do business.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: With the Industry Transformation Roadmaps and the myriad of support measures to help businesses transform, can MTI share the progress of companies in Singapore, including SMEs, in their business transformation?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: How will the various measures announced in Budget 2024 come together to support businesses, including SMEs, in their transformation efforts especially in digitalisation, cybersecurity, sustainability as well as growing internationally?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: How many Singapore companies have taken on the support measures to transform?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Mr Chairman, Singapore has retained our position as the world's leading business hub.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: But Singapore's hub status is challenged with increasing geopolitical uncertainties, emerging disruptive technologies and BEPS 2.0.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: What efforts is the Government making to ensure that Singapore continues to be attractive and competitive globally?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: As the hon Ms Mariam Jaafar has said, for MNEs to anchor their investments here, in Singapore, it is not an easy decision and it is extremely competitive.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: What strategies are we exploring to continue to make Singapore a place that the best global companies will choose to locate their regional and global businesses?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This is important for Singapore to have good growth as well as bring investments in cutting-edge technologies, know-how and good jobs.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Can more details be shared on international partnerships and how these partnerships can ensure that Singapore remains at the centre of global trade?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Leveraging on Singapore's status as a global business node, how can Singapore companies tap on the enhanced support measures announced in Budget 2024 to expand and capture growth opportunities to play an important role in regional and global value chains?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Neil Parekh, please take your two cuts together.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Chairman, in the Asia Pacific region, the digital economy, including AI and the green economy, present immense growth opportunities.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: My question for the Ministry is: how does MTI plan to continue supporting our enterprises and capture future growth opportunities in the region and growth sectors, such as AI and the green economy?

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: At the same time, given the promising growth potential in Southeast Asia, how does MTI plan to strengthen Singapore's links and collaborations with the region for new growth opportunities in green economy and AI, so that our businesses and people can tap on the opportunities beyond our shores?

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Chairman, as we navigate through an increasingly interconnected global economy, we must recognise that our nation's growth is intricately linked to our ability to venture beyond our shores.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore, although small in size, possesses boundless potential.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: But to fully unlock it, internationalisation becomes not just a choice but a necessity for sustained economic growth.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: However, the lingering effects of the pandemic, geopolitical tensions and the macroeconomic uncertainty have given rise to an increasingly fragmented world.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: There are headwinds to economic growth with high inflation rates and increasing volatility in the world.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: In Singapore, we have achieved quite a bit thus far.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Moving forward, Singapore needs to identify new opportunities and build new engines of growth as well as continue to build on our international partnerships.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: My question for the Ministry is: how can MTI continue facilitating our companies' endeavours to seize new economic opportunities in the fast-growing markets in Southeast Asia, South Asia, Latin America, Central Asia, the Middle East and Africa?

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Also, how do we protect the investments of Singaporean companies in these emerging markets?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Mr Chairman, in his Budget speech, Deputy Prime Minister Wong shared that the international environment has darkened dramatically – major powers are prioritising national security over economic interdependence in this current geopolitical climate and there are other potential headwinds, like BEPS 2.0, that may affect Singapore's competitiveness to attract investments.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In light of this, how do our global FTAs remain relevant and create conditions for cross-border investments and boost Singapore's competitiveness?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Ms He Ting Ru, please take your two cuts together.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Not necessarily because of anything we may have done but because major powers and others believe that it is possible to force us into certain positions.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We have seen US limits on technology transfers helm in some of the world's ability to export.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: During the Trump Administration, Singapore was placed on a list of potential currency manipulators that could face sanction.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: China has published a list of countries from Australia to Czechia from Canada to Japan and South Korea for acting in ways that it does not like.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This may get worse of shifts and domestic politics in China and the US.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: After all, any such plans must involve active public and business participation, sooner rather than later, to be effective.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The European Union (EU) is currently proposing a law, which requires larger companies to identify actual or potential negative impacts on human rights and their supply chain; and to prevent, mitigate and remedy these impacts.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This is on top of existing laws that already require large companies to perform due diligence on supply chains to ensure that they have a plan of vigilance to identify risks relating the labour practices, health and safety or environmental issues.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Our policies relating to recruitment fees have an impact in Singapore's ability to attract investment and business, particularly in sectors like the maritime industry, where companies have to employ many migrant workers.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: What are the reputational and legal risks for companies in the development of the Ministry of Manpower's (MOM's) policies and allocation of resources for enforcement?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Agreement has been reached between the European Parliament and Council and we are likely to see further progress on rules enforcing labour rights in global supply chains soon.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: These are seen to foster a business environment with legal certainty, a level playing field and sustainable competition that does not benefit from worker exploitation.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: In 2019, the International Labour Organization (ILO) governing body approved the definition of recruitment fees and related costs, emphasising that recruitment fee should not be borne by workers or jobseekers, as workers must not be required to pay for access to employment or it takes time for workforce structures to change.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: There are international standards ready for adoption by EU legislators and EU-based MNCs.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This is an area of concern, given the risk of debt bondage to workers' rights as well as their practical ability to make economic decisions, such as a choice to leave a job with poor working conditions.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I note the response to a Parliamentary Question last year that we are considering facilitating direct recruitment channels for returning workers.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Mark Lee, you can take both your cuts together.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: These offshore activities will ultimately contribute to tangible and intangible assets that benefit Singapore, enabling our businesses to reduce costs and maximise value capture.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Will MTI consider revising current grant schemes to include coverage for business expenses incurred during offshore development activities?

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: This adjustment can significantly aid local companies in leveraging international resources while ensuring the resulting benefits bolster Singapore's economy.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Local businesses have shared their struggle to retain and develop talent because MNEs and aiming to swiftly expand their operations, often offer high and yet unsustainable wages to fulfill their foreign worker quotas, disadvantage SMEs in talent development and acquisition.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Given these concerns, how does MTI plan to nurture our local SMEs to navigate these challenges effectively?

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong
text: Chairman, in recent years, particularly in the wake of the global pandemic, SMEs have faced unprecedented challenges that have tested their resilience, adaptability and sustainability.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong
text: MTI has been instrumental in introducing various support measures to aid these enterprises as they navigate the complexities of recovery and seek new opportunities for growth.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong
text: As such, how will the Government continue to support these SMEs?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Mr Chairman, Sir, before the onset of the pandemic, considerable efforts were dedicated to assisting our local enterprises in seizing opportunities abroad and expanding their global footprint.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As we transition from the pandemic, the external landscape and supply chains have undergone significant shifts due to the heightened emphasis on resilience and geopolitical tensions, leading to increased polarisation and "friend-shoring".

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Moreover, considering MTI's success in securing Foreign Direct Investments in recent years and the presence of MNEs, how will these factors empower local businesses to capitalise on emerging opportunities?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Will this integration be part of the enhanced PACT programme and if so, what is the synergy between Scale-up and PACT?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Furthermore, MTI's proactive approach to signing FTAs with various jurisdictions presents additional opportunities for local enterprises to expand its overseas revenues.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: How does MTI facilitate local businesses in seizing these opportunities?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: What contributions do trade associations and chambers (TACs) make in this regard and how is MTI enhancing its support to TACs to bolster secretariat manpower and capabilities further?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Another area that has changed post-pandemic is the tourism landscape.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Businesses operating within the tourism and related sectors are encountering notable challenges stemming from several factors.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: One, escalating manpower costs due to tight labour markets.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Three, sluggish recovery of tourism arrivals from key traditional markets.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And four, strengthening of the Singapore dollar against key tourism markets.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: What are MTIs strategies to mitigate these challenges?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Competing markets have also unveiled substantial new initiatives and attractions, vying for a share of the tourism market.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: The year 2023 saw the breakthrough of AI and its use cases in the real world.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: But as is always said, AI will not replace humans but the person using AI will.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: In essence, SMEs who will succeed better are those that can adapt and transform quicker, by viewing digitalisation and AI as a friend instead of a foe.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: As a practitioner using various forms of AI, including GenAI, in my work to sharpen effectiveness and productivity in risk management and auditing, I can understand why SMEs may face and see AI as intimidating.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: There is a need to help SMEs dispel a "fear of the unknown" and the notion that AI is reserved only for MNEs.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: On sustainability, I am glad that Budget 2024 has covered key aspects of going green as a competitive advantage, because MNEs have started on their sustainability journey earlier and would expect the same for our own SME suppliers.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: I am also glad to learn that SMEs in more sectors will benefit from green loans and the Energy Efficiency Grant, which I had asked for at last year's Committee of Supply debate and Government support to be more inclusive.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Many cite having to navigate complex reporting standards as a hurdle.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: While opportunities in the digital and green economy are aplenty, we know that transformation is not easy and more funding on its own is not sufficient.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: What matters more fundamentally, is for SMEs to shift their mindsets and be willing to accelerate their efforts.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: For those who are, they should be provided with ready-access to expertise.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: This is where SME Centres and TACs, as critical nexus for engagement and advisory, can play a more proactive role to nudge and help SMEs digitalise and go green.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: In my engagement with the industry, a feedback suggested by SMEs was for such Centres to go beyond the marketing of grant options and providing generic guidance; and offer more in terms of business development advice and more customised expertise and guidance.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: As such, can MTI share on three areas.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Two, whether TACs can be guided to deepen understanding of their own members' profile to provide more targeted facilitation and support as well as more effective cross-learning between its members?

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Thirdly, whether we can build a more comprehensive support ecosystem for SMEs, such as by (a) synergising the roles of SME Centres and TACs with the enhanced Partnerships for Capability Transformation Scheme for SMEs to connect more easily to learn digital and green strategies; (b) deepening collaborations with Institutes of Higher Learning for training; and (c) leveraging clan associations with wide business connections for advocacy.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: Yet, businesses struggle to scale up AI beyond pilots and POCs and therefore fail to derive value and impact from their efforts.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: As I spoke about in my Budget debate speech and again, I would like to declare my interest as a Managing Director and Senior Partner of a consulting firm that does the work of AI.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: Scaling AI requires more than just buying a platform and hiring a few data scientists.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: I spoke about the 10-20-70 rule: 10% of the effort is in the algorithms; 20% in the technological and IT foundations – the infrastructure, the data architecture; 70% though, is about people and processes – ways of working, business-process reinvention, how to drive adoption at scale, organisation, talent strategy and change management.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: Businesses therefore need to move beyond experimentation and POCs.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: They need to have a clear strategy and roadmap of how they will build the AI platform, data, process, organisation and other enablers and sequence the development of use cases so that they are able to fund their AI transformation journey and win in the medium-term.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: How will the Government now help organisations take the next steps to implement AI at-scale, beyond POCs and pilots?

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Mr Chairman, retrenchments and redundancies are expected to continue.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: MNEs, Lazada, Amazon and Google in the technological sector have reduced staff.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: From time to time, local enterprises also succumb to changing conditions and downsize or cease operations.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: We need to continually find new foreign investments and also keep building up and strengthening local businesses.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: The local business sector was built over the decades, possibly centuries, by individuals with the entrepreneurial spirit.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: While the majority are classified SMEs, we also have large successful local enterprises and collectively, these employ many Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: My question to the Ministry and to all of us is: what will we do to keep the entrepreneurial spirit thriving, especially in challenging times and when business conditions may not be conducive?

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Also, with Forward Singapore (Forward SG), there may well be a resurgence in social entrepreneurial initiatives.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: How can we support these agents of change?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: Incentives and grants are critical in providing seed support and are crucial in driving SME growth and are important signals in the industrial strategy we are developing, especially for our green transition.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: The survey also said that apart from grants, SMEs feel they need more support in areas ranging from subsidies for talent and acquisition schemes, indicative of the tight labour market, more support for international expansion and rental assistance and rental support.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: The same survey also found that a streamlined grant application process was on the wishlist.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: We should continue to simplify the adoption process for grants and in particular, green grants.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: For many SMEs, daily operations are a priority and not grant applications and associated administrative work.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: Perhaps, one way to improve the system would be for Enterprise Singapore to provide a one-stop web page offering advice and guidance to SMEs on how they can green their business and what the associated grants are.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: Also important, are the money itself and the time value of money.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: Additionally, in order to properly understand whether our grants are properly supporting our SMEs, we should publicly announce how we track their success.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: For example, alongside how much has been disbursed for green grants, we should state how many tonnes of emissions have been mitigated per dollar spent, so that the public, civil society and Members of Parliament can be sure that these taxpayer-paid subsidies are working; and to measure how they have achieved their goals.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: Other commentators have noted that the lack of standardised measurement in reporting standards have made the environmental, social and governance (ESG) compliance efforts challenging for SMEs.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: I hope that we would study how to tackle mental health and well-being at work in the context of our smaller enterprises in order to understand the particular challenges that they face and to ultimately develop interventions that are targeted to work to raise the well-being of our workers in SMEs; and see if any interventions can be made beyond those which currently form part of MOM's Total Workplace Safety and Health programme.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee
text: Could MTI provide insights into EEG’s effectiveness in these areas, highlight successful strategies and share lessons to encourage broader uptake across newly included sectors?

speaker: Mr Mark Lee
text: Furthermore, in recognising beyond financial and technical hurdles SMEs encounter in adopting energy-efficient practices, is there a consideration from MTI to expand EEG to encompass a more holistic support package, covering consultancy, execution and training costs, to facilitate in this transition?

speaker: Mr Mark Lee
text: Moreover, in the context of shifting towards clean energy and the high associated costs, can MTI outline any assistance for SMEs, particularly in adopting electric vehicles for commercial and industrial use?

speaker: Mr Mark Lee
text: Lastly, could MTI explain the exclusion of crucial sectors like Process and Logistics from EEG, given their importance in decarbonisation, and are there plans to integrate these sectors into the programme?

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong
text: The vitality of our heartland enterprises is indispensable to the socio-economic fabric of our nation, serving not just the backbone of our local economy but also the heartbeat of our community life.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong
text: As such, can MTI provide an update on the support measures for heartland enterprises under this initiative?

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: Chairman, in today's world, where large retail chains and online shopping platforms dominate the market, our neighborhood shops are facing unprecedented challenges.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: Yet, these small establishments offer something invaluable that transcends mere commerce – they are the lifelines of our localities.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: Our heartland enterprises provide a unique social value that nurtures the spirit of our communities.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: These are places where personal connections are made, where the shopkeepers know your name, family and preferences.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: These businesses, often run by families and local entrepreneurs, are deeply rooted in the community.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: They contribute to the local community, create jobs and frequently offer personalised services that larger stores cannot.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: Therefore, it is crucial that the Government proactively step in to support these vital community assets.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: These initiatives are crucial in helping our neighborhood shops sharpen their competitive edge and carve out a distinct role for them to thrive in the years to come.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: There are a fair number of heartland F&B and retail shops in my constituency of Toa Payoh East, most notably around the Lorong 8 Market and Hawker Centre, and Kim Keat Food Centre.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The charm of these open, ground floor establishments cannot be replicated by our shopping malls and complexes, not to mention the convenience that they offer to the seniors living in the neighbourhood.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua
text: Mr Chairman, trade associations played a valuable role during COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua
text: These included closely working with the Government and Members, providing input on business realities and proposing ways to ride through the pandemic and to retain jobs.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua
text: Historically, trade associations have brought like-minded businesses by sector to work cooperatively, share best practices, improve productivity and, in many instances, to internationalise.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua
text: Recovery from COVID-19 has been patchy for some sectors and many continue to face the recent challenges of higher costs across many fronts.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua
text: Trade associations will remain relevant, though some sectors may face consolidation while others see opportunities for growth.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua
text: The broad-based Budget support measures will help many companies.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua
text: How will MTI best support trade associations in this challenging phase of global and domestic business disruption?

speaker: Mr Keith Chua
text: How will MTI approach those sectors and their trade associations that see consolidation but still remain viable?

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong
text: Chairman, in the intricate tapestry of our nation's economy, trade associations and chambers (TACs) stand out as pivotal enablers that bolster the capabilities, reach and resilience of our businesses across various sectors.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong
text: By offering a platform for advocacy, sharing best practices and facilitating collaborations, TACs play a crucial role in the upliftment and sustainability of businesses, particularly SMEs that form the backbone of our economy.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong
text: As such, what are we doing to ensure that TACs are sufficiently equipped to play this role effectively?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Mr Chairman, our manufacturing sector is a key part of our Singapore Economy 2030 vision.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Our strategy is to attract frontier investments into Singapore to create good manufacturing jobs for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Being a country with natural resource constraints, our higher land, labour and transport costs make it challenging for global manufacturers.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: We do not want to draw a manufacturing giant in only to lose them five to 10 years later to cheap countries which have caught up in technology and know-how.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Can the Government share more about its plans to enhance the competitiveness of the manufacturing sector, keep them here, and how our local companies can benefit from these plans?

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong
text: Chairman, the marine and offshore engineering sector has long been a cornerstone of our nation's industrial landscape, contributing significantly to our economic development and global trade capabilities.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong
text: However, in the face of evolving global energy demands, technological advancements and the urgency for sustainability, there is a pressing need to transform and future-proof this vital sector.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong
text: As such, can the Government share more on how the industry transformation plans to assist the marine and offshore engineering sector?

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant
text: Chairman, the tourism industry is vital for our economy.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant
text: As a key pillar of our economy, the tourism industry, besides creating jobs and opportunities for our citizens, also enhances our international brand as a global business hub with a vibrant lifestyle.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant
text: As we move into a new world after the pandemic, it remains crucial for Singapore to continue to capture the tourism market.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant
text: Can MTI please provide an update on the tourism revitalisation efforts?

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant
text: What will MTI do to ensure that Singapore remains an attractive tourist destination amidst growing global competition?

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Chairman, taking deliberate steps to infuse Singapore firms with the capabilities of Singapore’s creative professionals in arts, culture, media and design is the game changer that can bring forth an industry renaissance.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Like how the advent of the printing press led to unprecedented change, digital technology and AI are initiating new ways to produce and trade.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Thus, if technology and AI are the tools that a firm uses to reimagine its operating model, then a creative lens must be what a firm applies to redefine its business model.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: To engender the meeting of minds between progressive firms and creative freelancers, I offer three possibilities for the Minister’s consideration.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: First, would the Ministry work closely with NTUC’s Visual, Audio, Creative Content Professionals Association (VACCPA) and relevant sector agencies to develop and share use cases of when and how firms could tap Singapore's different creative forms to create new value?

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: For instance, retailers could tap freelancers to create novel, virtual shopping experience using 3-D digital asset creation.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Economic funding schemes could be expanded to cater for such creative use cases.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Second, could the Ministry expand the SkillsFuture Enterprise Credit to cater to creative micro-firms of one to two persons?

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Last, could the Ministry facilitate opportunities for creative freelancers to work and learn on international projects supported by the economic agencies?

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: For instance, opportunity could be created for Singaporean freelance lighting designers to augment international touring acts courted to Singapore.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Such stints can be underpinned by robust hiring and accreditation and the relevant Tripartite Standards.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Freelancers would appreciate the boost to their development and portfolio.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Through these three possibilities, Singapore businesses and creative freelancers can unlock synergies and develop new competitive advantage to stay ahead of change and global competition.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Mr Chairman, Singapore has a vibrant and flourishing creative economy which includes sectors, such as the arts and culture, media and design.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: MCCY has also stated that in the coming years, the outlook for the creative economy in Singapore is positive.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: According to MCCY, while the growth of the sector depends on many factors, there are opportunities for creative practitioners, especially if they are able to capitalise on growing demands and trends.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: This includes the leveraging of technology and working with regional and international partners to reach audiences beyond Singapore.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: MCCY also provided assurance that the Government will continue to provide support to help the sector grow by injecting funding, providing skills development opportunities and brokering partnerships with the private sector to open up opportunities for creatives.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: For example, will any significant expenditure be incurred by the Singapore Tourism Board for the promotion of tourist consumption of Singapore arts?

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Will EDB and Enterprise Singapore be working on any specific projects or plans in the coming financial year that are related to the development and growth of our creative economy?

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: If there are any specific plans underway related to the creative economy, can the Ministry share the particular areas of focus?

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong
text: Chairman, R&D fuels the creation of new products, services and processes, enabling businesses to innovate and stay ahead of competition.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong
text: This continuous innovation is essential for sustaining long-term economic growth, as it leads to the development of unique offerings that meet emerging consumer needs and adapt to changing market conditions.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong
text: Through R&D, companies and economies can find new methods of production, utilise resources more efficiently and improve operational processes.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong
text: It also encourages entrepreneurship by providing the knowledge base and technological advancements necessary for the creation of startups.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong
text: As such, what are some R&D initiatives and sectors that MTI will be focusing on to grow our Singapore economy?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: The additional funding will go towards research and related investments in national priorities, which include deepening our capability in advanced manufacturing, sustainability, the digital economy and healthcare.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: Can MTI share the progress of the RIE2025 plan since its launch in 2020?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: What initiatives will MTI be focusing on to build Singapore's innovative capability to grow our economy?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: How will we grow the talent pool in Singapore to help bring these innovations to market and strengthen the capabilities of our enterprises?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: During the Budget debate, Deputy Prime Minister Heng Swee Keat spoke about the importance of building greater linkages and collaboration at all levels and of the innovation ecosystems.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: Can more be shared about these innovation ecosystems and the impact for Singapore as an innovation and business hub?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant: Chairman, science and technology are instrumental to Singapore's survival and success and has helped us overcome the constraints of our small size and somewhat limited resources.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: The RIE ecosystem remains a cornerstone of Singapore's development into a knowledge-based, innovation-driven economy and society.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: The RIE's ecosystem is also a key enabler in creating new avenues of growth and raising Singapore's economic competitiveness.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: The recent announcements by Deputy Prime Minister Wong during the 2024 Budget have underscored our Government's commitment to fostering innovation and driving research and development initiatives to propel our economy forward.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: A key area of Singapore's research and development efforts would be unlocking new economic opportunities and helping Singapore's economy and businesses transform to remain competitive.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: This could include new opportunities in advanced manufacturing, health technology and emerging areas, like AI.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: R&D can also enable companies' green transition and our push towards greater sustainability.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: My questions for the Ministry are: first, can MTI share some of the research and development initiatives and sectors the Ministry will focus on to grow our economy?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: Also, how does MTI plan to leverage on research and development to tap into promising growth sectors and facilitate Singapore's transition to a low-carbon economy?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Mr Chairman, besides labour, capital and enterprise, land is an important scarce resource for Singapore as a small country.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: It is difficult to imagine that the land where Marina Bay Sands (MBS) stands today was all sea until the Marina Bay area was reclaimed from 1992 to 2004.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: But our maritime boundaries and our shipping hub status means there is a limit to how much we can claim further land from the sea.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Hence, we have been deliberate about allocating scarce land to our competing land needs, through our Concept Plan and Master Plan.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: In 2021, it was announced that the review of Singapore's long-term land use plans will also need to cater for uncertainties, such as land buffers, which can be quickly converted for contingency uses.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: How can we optimise our land use and unlock our resource potential?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: Singapore has set very ambitious plans to achieve net-zero emissions by 2050.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: As a small country with limited renewable energy potential, it is challenging to balance delivering sustainable, secure and affordable energy.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: The Singapore Energy Transition (SET) was launched in 2021 as a blueprint laying out the broad plans for the power sector to decarbonise and help Singapore achieve its climate commitments.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: The SET involves using natural gas more sustainably, maximising solar deployment, introducing regional power grids and electricity imports; and preparing for deep decarbonisation using hydrogen and emerging low-carbon alternatives.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: Can MTI share the progress of Singapore's plans to decarbonise our power sector?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: Is Singapore making other investments to green our power sectors with sources of low-carbon alternatives?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: What are the key initiatives that will be invested in to catalyse Singapore's transition to clean energy?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Chairman, all the energy that powers life on Earth today ultimately comes from the Sun.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And so, what if we can replicate that energy production in the core of the Sun, here on Earth?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: This, simplistically, is the promise of fusion energy.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: I must clarify that nuclear fusion is completely different from nuclear fission.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Fusion does not produce the same radioactive waste; does not risk meltdowns; and does not entail dependence on other countries for fuel, such as uranium.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Given the advantages of fusion, I hope that when we say we are studying the option of nuclear energy in our future clean energy mix, our bet is weighted towards fusion energy.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And I will go further, to say that while we can and will import clean energy, through regional grids and/or hydrogen, ultimately, energy imports may not be enough and not secure enough for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And so, I think we will need domestically produced fusion energy to secure our clean energy future in the long term.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Furthermore, our net-zero target is 2050 and Deputy Prime Minister Wong has also said that we will take the next 20 years to build our clean energy mix.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: So, one could argue that we have some time, and should take some time, to decide if we want to adopt fusion.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: But that is only considering the energy security standpoint.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: From an economic standpoint, because fusion does also presents tremendous economic opportunities for Singapore and the world, we actually have a lot less time to decide.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And paradoxically, precisely because the technology is not yet mature, we should move fast.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: To paraphrase my Jurong colleague, Dr Tan Wu Meng, we can be the first mover or we can find ourselves too late to move.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Fusion technology has made major strides in the last two years and the real breakthroughs could come in the next five years with what the industry calls "net energy production".

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: This will put on track the first utility-scale plants to be constructed in the early-to-mid 2030s.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Countries around the world have started to make serious moves in fusion.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: So, if we start now, there is already catching up to do with the leaders.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: But if we do it right, Singapore could become the Asia-Pacific manufacturing hub for fusion machines.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: This would mean a whole suite of new, exciting jobs for Singaporeans – the next generation of fusion scientists, engineers and operators, all designing and making the technology that will power the world in future.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: To get there, we need to do three things now.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: First, lead and support our universities, research institutes and local SMEs to build capabilities to get into the fusion supply chain, get into the fusion supply chain now for prototypes and pilot plants; second, work with leading countries to design fusion-specific regulations; and third, importantly, we need to feature fusion energy in our 2050 energy roadmap to formally set the ambition for ourselves and to signal to the global fusion community that Singapore wants to be a player and wants to contribute.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: On nuclear fusion, we should dream big, start now and signal strong.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee
text: As Deputy Prime Minister Lawrence Wong highlighted, transitioning to green energy necessitates substantial investments in infrastructure and technology, supported by Government-led catalytic funding.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee
text: Given this context, I am seeking clarification is the Government planning to work with these businesses who are engaged in these initiatives and will the Ministry consider leveraging the Future Energy Fund to enhance the financial viability of these ongoing projects?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: Mr Chairman, I would speak on addressing our energy constraints while meeting our climate commitments.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: This is crucial for our economy and environment.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: In addition, it is essential to improve the efficiency of electricity generation, storage and transmission.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: Hence, what are MTI's plans to modernise our energy grid to efficiently integrate diverse sources of energy and improve overall efficiency?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: In addition, how will the modernisation of the energy grid be financed and what are the cost implications to consumers and businesses?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: So, what is MTI's projection of future energy needs to support the growth of our digital economy, especially in the domain of AI?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: As the cooling demands in data centres and chip manufacturing facilities contribute significantly to the overall electrical consumption, what measures are being taken to optimise cooling in Singapore?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: Furthermore, with the escalating temperatures induced by climate change, Singapore faces heightened electricity usage for cooling purposes.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: I have highlighted in this Chamber – Singapore's strides in developing District Cooling Systems and their advantages.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: Are there plans to intensify efforts in this domain and cultivate local enterprises to bolster their capabilities in this sector and export this expertise to other global regions?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: In Budget 2024, the Government announced an expansion of the Energy Efficiency Grant (EEG).

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: However, we need to evaluate the effectiveness of such programmes.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: Furthermore, considering the potential for significant systemic impact, I would like to ask whether there is room for additional upstream energy efficiency grants targeting plants, buildings and districts.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: Such upstream savings could have substantial benefits to the overall energy conservation efforts.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: The $5 billion FEF is a positive step towards cleaner energy.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: However, it may not suffice for our clean energy transition.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: Will there be future top-ups or will the fund collaborate with borrowings, such as through the SINGA bonds?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: As we aim to reduce our carbon footprint and promote sustainable growth, our limited access to clean energy stands as a key limiting factor to economic growth.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: This could impact the real income growth and living standards of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: Hence, we must address our clean energy constraints.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Despite transformative changes in how consumers engage with businesses, the approach to safeguarding consumer rights in Singapore has not evolved, appearing to maintain a somewhat indifferent stance toward consumer protections.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: We only need to look at the many high-profile and recent consumer incidents in Singapore – from the Sentosa Sky Lantern Festival, the abrupt closure of gym franchises, the chronic overbooking of cruises and flights, errant renovation contractors, "lemons" in the used car trade and the unsatisfactory customer service that has become synonymous with certain carsharing and food courier operators.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: These are just a few of the specific areas which are found wanting when it comes to protecting the interests of consumers.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In many of these cases, you should not need a consumer association to tell you that businesses cannot just sell subscriptions and then shut down, leaving consumers with no recourse, or that a refund with "platform credits" is not quite the same as cash payments in kind, or that if an airline overbooks and is unable to accommodate your trip, it is solely on them to provide an acceptable alternative to the customers' satisfaction.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: While the Government has undertaken some initiatives to address unfair trading practices, it falls short of the robust protection framework that a first-world economy like Singapore should have.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: We need to transform the prevailing mindset of caveat emptor or buyer beware into one where individuals can confidently stand against the might of big business and know that the customer is not always right, but at least we will always be treated fairly.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Chairman, I declare my interest as President of CASE.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Price transparency is a core principle that safeguards our consumers and ensures that we make well-informed purchasing decisions.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: With MTI's support, CASE is prepared to assist retailers to implement unit pricing.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The most frequent issues pertain to failure to receive orders within delivery timeframes and failure to receive refunds.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: We must take urgent actions to better protect our consumers, particularly as purchasing behaviour has shifted and many consumers now rely on e-commerce.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: CASE stands ready to partner MTI on this so that we can all better protect consumers.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Chairman, let me first thank Members for their thoughtful comments.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The past few years have been very challenging.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: As a small and open economy, Singapore felt keenly the impact of uncertainties arising from the pandemic and structural shifts in the global economy.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: But we did not let this put us down.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We pressed on with our transformation journey and helped our businesses turn challenges into opportunities.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: During the COVID-19 pandemic, we experienced our worst recession since Independence.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Our top priority then was to support our companies through this unprecedented crisis and protect jobs for Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Even before the pandemic was over, new challenges surfaced.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Global food and energy prices rose sharply due to supply chain disruptions, which then led to global inflation.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Interest rates were raised, as central banks around the world sought to counter inflationary pressures.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Geopolitical contestation and strategic competition between major powers, such as the US and China intensified.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East erupted and there is a growing urgency to address climate change.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Nonetheless, our external environment remains volatile and uncertain, as several Members have pointed out.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Many businesses, especially SMEs, are concerned about increased business costs and access to financing.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: They have also asked for more support to pursue transformation and training to stay competitive and capture new opportunities.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The Package has three components: Corporate Income Tax Rebate to help with cash flow; adjustments to the Enterprise Financing Scheme to help businesses access loan financing; and an extension of the SkillsFuture Enterprise Credit to support transformation and skills training efforts.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: First, let me explain the Corporate Income Tax Rebate.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The corporate income tax rebate will benefit many enterprises, especially the SMEs.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Next, we will adjust the Enterprise Financing Scheme (EFS) that facilitates access to loan financing.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: During the pandemic, we significantly enhanced the EFS to provide stronger support for businesses.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We have since reviewed and adjusted the EFS to better suit current business needs.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: For example, internationalisation plans were significantly disrupted during the pandemic when global markets came to a standstill.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: To help companies sustain their efforts, we doubled the maximum loan quantum for the EFS-Trade Loan to $10 million and increased the Government's risk-share to 70%.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: One company that has used the EFS to internationalise is Apeiron Bioenergy, which produces clean fuel from waste products.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The company tapped on the EFS-Trade Loan and EFS-Green to deliver its first contract of used cooking oil, a clean biofuel feedstock to the US market and expand its facilities in Asia and the United Arab Emirates.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: As the global markets are still recovering, we will extend the enhanced maximum loan quantum of $10 million for one year until 31 March 2025, but at a 50% risk-sharing.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: This is in line with Mr Mark Lee's call to support Singapore businesses as they expand overseas.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: During the pandemic, we had also expanded the EFS-Project Loan scheme to include domestic construction projects which were badly affected.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Most construction projects are now back on schedule and the sector is generally recovering, although some companies are still facing challenges.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Hence, we will extend the support for domestic construction projects under EFS-Project Loan (Domestic) by one year until 31 March 2025 to help the industry, but at a lower maximum loan quantum of $15 million instead of $30 million.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: In addition, we will permanently increase the maximum loan quantum of the EFS-Working Capital Loan to $500,000.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We temporarily increased the cap during the pandemic when businesses were facing severe cash flow constraints.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Since then, while cash flow has improved, the working capital needs of SMEs have, in fact, increased, amidst the increased business volumes and costs.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Making the higher maximum loan quantum permanent will better support our SMEs.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Since 2020, more than 30,000 enterprises have utilised the SkillsFuture Enterprise Credit (SFEC) to support the training and upgrading of their employees and to pursue enterprise transformation.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: It used SFEC to offset costs of their digital workflow transformation project.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The company also used SFEC to send their employees for SkillsFuture training courses, ranging from human resource to drone piloting, to meet the company's needs.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: To allow businesses to benefit more from SFEC, we will extend the claims submission deadline by one year to 30 June 2025.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We will continue refining our support for enterprises to deepen workforce and enterprise transformation.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Minister of State Low Yen Ling will also speak about additional measures to specifically support our heartland enterprises.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: While we tackle near-term challenges, we must continue to invest in our longer-term future and build a resilient and vibrant economy.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: To achieve this, we need to be GUTC.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We will grow our economy through three key thrusts: leveraging our trade networks; promoting investment and the adoption of new technologies; and developing our talent.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Singapore is well-placed to benefit from growth in our region and beyond.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Our extensive connectivity has been and will continue to be our key competitive advantage.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Singapore has established a strong reputation as a well-connected, reliable and trusted logistics and transportation hub.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Amid shifts in global supply chains, businesses and investors continue to be attracted to Singapore due to our robust infrastructure, pro-business policies and skilled workforce.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: To sustain our economic growth, Singapore, as a small economy, cannot afford to turn away from the global market; nor can we have the global market turn away from us.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Mr Liang Eng Hwa, Ms Jessica Tan and Mr Sharael Taha asked what the Government is doing to ensure Singapore will remain competitive and attractive to global investors.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: For a start, we must expand international and regional connectivity by continuing to strengthen the rules-based trading architecture, to widen our economic space and tap on global opportunities.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: This will allow us to evolve innovative trade cooperation models across different geographies, enlarge our community of trading partners and establish connections with new markets.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We will continue to deepen cooperation with our global partners to grow trade and attract investments.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We will engage our partners through current platforms, like the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership and the Indo-Pacific Economic Framework for Prosperity, as well as via bilateral partnerships, like the US-Singapore Partnership for Growth and Innovation, China-Singapore FTA and the India-Singapore Ministerial Roundtable.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Closer to home, the Southeast Asian region is projected to grow more quickly than the global economy over the next five years.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: ASEAN, as a grouping, is also strengthening external relations with our partners.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Under Indonesia's Chairmanship last year, ASEAN concluded negotiations to upgrade the ASEAN-Australia-New Zealand FTA.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We are currently negotiating an FTA with Canada, as well as upgrading and reviewing ASEAN's Agreements with China and India.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We have also stepped up cooperation with our immediate neighbours.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: For example, we are exploring the establishment of a Johor-Singapore Special Economic Zone to bolster our economic cooperation with Malaysia and Johor.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) in January this year and agreed to work towards improving cross-border flows in goods, people and investments.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Mr Liang Eng Hwa, Ms Foo Mee Har and Mr Neil Parekh asked how MTI intends to capture future growth opportunities.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: This is a tax credit with a refundable cash feature.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: RIC will support qualified firms in developing high-value and substantive economic activities in Singapore, such as the setting up of manufacturing facilities or an expansion of these facilities, commodity trading, R&D and innovation as well as decarbonisation activities.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: As pointed out by Ms Mariam Jaafar, the RIC will bolster our competitiveness in attracting and anchoring quality investments to create more opportunities and good jobs for Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We will also help our companies ride the global wave of technological advancement and pursue opportunities in new growth areas, such as advanced manufacturing, AI and sustainability.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: By being early movers and adopters, we can sharpen our companies' competitive edge, capture the rapid growth of these new markets and develop world-leading enterprises.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Manufacturing is a key pillar of our economy.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: As Mr Saktiandi Supaat has noted, it contributes about one-fifth of our GDP and employs about one-eighth of our workforce.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We will double down on our strengths in robotics and automation to target high-value opportunities in advanced manufacturing and secure new growth pathways.
