text: This council provides funding and coaching for design research and product development, partners with companies to adopt design for business growth, and nurtures industry-ready design talent.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Ms Jean See also highlighted the potential of harnessing creative talent to redefine businesses.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: In addition to DesignSingapore’s efforts, broad-based schemes such as our Enterprise Development Grant (EDG) will allow businesses to engage creative professionals to build their strategic brand as well as their marketing capability.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: We expect this to boost arrivals and spending across our retail, F&B, and tourism-related sectors.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: This longer visa exemption has made it more convenient for Singaporeans to travel to China for leisure and business, boosting two-way traffic.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: As we continue to put Singapore on the world map, we welcome people from all around the world – not just as a tourist destination, but also as a business hub.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Minister Gan shared how our trade networks help grow our economy.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: I will focus on how we are extending our connections to be a stronger and more vibrant business node.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Mr Neil Parekh emphasised the importance of trade to Singapore given our very small size and small domestic market.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Amidst growing geopolitical tensions and protectionist trade policies, which was also a concern raised by Ms He Ting Ru, we must continue to strengthen Singapore’s global trade competitiveness.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Mr Parekh asked how we are helping companies to seize new opportunities in growing markets.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Well, my MTI colleagues and I have been travelling the world to strengthen these economic ties.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: We are uncovering new markets, new business opportunities and new partners for our many companies.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Some of these journeys are 30 hours one way, but they are worth doing even though they are very tiring.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: And I will be making more of these trips this year because Minister Gan has asked me to.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: But let me take you around the world from a trade and also a business lens.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: First stop: let us go to India, a country I visited a few times last year.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: We continue to advance our collaborations with India, which the World Economic Forum projects to be the world’s third largest economy by 2030.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: It is already the world’s most populous nation and one of its youngest too.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Between 2012 and 2022, Singapore’s investments into India grew by more than five times.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: In 2022, India was Singapore’s 11th largest trading partner and India will remain a key market of strategic importance to Singapore.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: At the inaugural India-Singapore Ministerial Roundtable in 2022, our countries identified five mutually beneficial areas of collaboration.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: And we have started to see some fruits of success from this work.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: This showcases how digital tech can make international trade easier and also more accessible.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: We are also helping our students gain greater exposure to India’s markets.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Enterprise Singapore, in partnership with the Confederation of Indian Industry (CII) announced the India Ready Talent (IRT) internship programme in February 2024.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: IRT offers our University and Polytechnic students internship opportunities in India to deepen their understanding of India’s business environment.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: From India let us travel to Latin America – a region I have been travelling to extensively over the last few years: Minister Vivian Balakrishnan and I were just in Brazil in December to sign a new FTA with the MERCOSUR.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: To date, more than 150 Singapore companies have commercial interests in Latin America.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: This builds on the FTA we signed with the Pacific Alliance bloc in 2022, which comprises Chile, Colombia, Mexico and Peru.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: From India and Latin America, let us now travel to the Middle East and Africa.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: During Prime Minister's visit to Saudi Arabia and the UAE in October 2023, we signed several agreements including MOUs on recognition of halal certifications.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Singapore companies can now look forward to exporting halal food products to both countries.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Africa is the most youthful population in the world and by 2050, more than a quarter of the world’s population will be African.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Last year, I joined Prime Minister Lee on his visit to Africa, where we signed agreements with South Africa and Kenya.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: In August, we hosted African business and political leaders at the 7th Africa Singapore Business Forum (ABSF) organised by Enterprise Singapore.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: This business forum attracted over 500 delegates and connected 200 businesses from Asia to Africa to explore collaborations while using Singapore as a node to facilitate Asia-African trade.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: SBF led business delegations to many of these regions and we met with them on the ground.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: They were there to explore commercial opportunities and I invite more companies to join SBF and other business delegations to expand their reach into these very promising and high potential emerging markets.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Beyond FTAs, we are also pioneering new agreements in new growth engines.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: We now have four Digital Economy Agreements (DEAs), to facilitate end-to-end digital trade by promoting the use of digital tools, enabling open and secure data flows and building trust in digital systems.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: We also developed Green Economy Agreements (GEAs) to support emissions reduction while spurring economic growth and also create jobs in the green economy.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Our GEA with Australia has catalysed collaborations in scientific research, green shipping corridors, and co-innovation programmes for SMEs and we invite more companies to join us along this green journey.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Through our journey around the world, we explored abundant opportunities for our companies back home.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Mr Edward Chia asked how we are using these agreements.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: This leads me to my second point of how we are helping our companies internationalise and also enter these growth markets.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: As an open economy, our firms are inevitably exposed to global supply chains impact.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Ms He Ting Ru pointed out that Singapore companies are therefore having to deal with new risks.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: We note that she has asked specific questions on manpower which we will defer to the Ministry of Manpower to address at this point.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: But the point is we cannot fully shield our companies from these risks, but we can provide financing for them and help them to build their capabilities.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: For example, they can use our Market Readiness Assistance (MRA) and the Enterprise Development Grant (EDG) to defray the cost of venturing outside and exploring these new markets.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: We also offer a 200% tax deductible on eligible expenses for international market expansion and investment development activities through our Double Tax Deduction for Internationalisation (DTDi) scheme.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Mr Desmond Choo would be pleased to know that there are many success stories from our work in helping Singapore companies internationalise.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: One such company is iFAST, which is a homegrown fintech firm that provides investment products and services, digital banking and pension administration services. iFAST designed a customer acquisition and onboarding strategy for iFAST Global Bank (iGB), a UK-based digital bank and developed a go-to-market strategy to strengthen its regional presence. iFAST aims to reach $100 billion of assets under administration by 2030.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: We look forward to more of such success stories to strengthen Singapore companies’ presence worldwide.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Beyond signing agreements and encouraging companies to internationalise, we are also pursuing new trade flows in areas such as carbon credits as well as biofuels.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: We have built a vibrant carbon services and trading ecosystem for our companies.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Today, there are over 120 carbon services and trading firms in Singapore, an increase from 70 since 2020.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: There are new entrants including firms like Bain & Company which has established its Global Sustainability Innovation Centre here in Singapore, and the International Emissions Trading Association (IETA) which opened its Asia hub here last year.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Our strong network of energy and agri-commodities traders makes us home to a growing pool of companies that trade biofuels and its feedstock, such as Mewah, which sells biodiesel globally.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: To do all that we set out to do, we need the resources to provide and care for people and set them on a strong footing for the future.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: That is why the work that MTI does is so important.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
text: Much as I would like to sample the oolong tea that Minister of State Low Yen Ling recommended, I do have one question for Minister Tan See Leng.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
text: I can understand that we need this terminal to strengthen our energy resilience.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
text: We already depend heavily on piped gas and, therefore, we will need also to have, as a backup, LNG.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
text: But can I ask the Minister how MTI sees the planned time horizon for this second LNG terminal?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
text: I ask this because, directionally, we are heading towards greener and cleaner energy.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
text: So, how would this second LNG terminal feature in our overall energy strategy, in terms of having greener and cleaner energy?

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: And we have two main sources – piped natural gas, which is from our neighbours, and LNG.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: As I have shared earlier on in my COS speech, the energy needs, the electrification needs, with the newer industries, FDIs coming in with the growth of our industries, as well as the SMEs' growth, these energy needs will continue to increase and not decrease.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, that gives us an added measure of security.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: On top of that, as I have also shared earlier on energy transition in the COS speech, a number of the other pathways and initiatives that we are pursuing, whether it is the Low Carbon Energy Research (LCER) programme for hydrogen, or embarking on pathfinder projects for ammonia and hydrogen, these are actually still relatively nascent.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: There are also the other measures that we are looking at whether it is geothermal, or also other types of advanced nuclear energy technology, including fusion energy.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I hope that answers the Member's query and his apprehensions as well.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: In the area of promoting collaboration between larger companies and SMEs, I had asked whether the Government would consider integrating the involvement of Singapore-based SMEs as a positive criterion for MNEs and also the large corporations when they access Government grants.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: This is really to make sure that, especially in the area of high-value investments, such as R&D and innovation-related grants, the Government-backed programmes can extend to a broader ecosystem.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: So, if Minister can say whether we can insert that little requirement.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: My second clarification is to Minister of State Low Yen Ling.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: I join Member Liang Eng Hwa in congratulating her for her enthusiasm in promoting innovation in the heartlands.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: But I want to ask a more pointed question, specifically.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: I explained in my COS speech, that actually for the specific schemes like PACT, the collaboration is with the local SMEs.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: So, that is already naturally part and parcel of the scheme design that we encourage large companies, MNCs, may be LLEs, to work with their suppliers.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: And some of these MNCs, large enterprises, are actually now beginning to go overseas, and they are quite keen to bring along their suppliers to go overseas too.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: And they also need to level up their capability in order to partner them in overseas markets.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: So, this programme is very useful in nurturing collaboration between large companies and local SMEs.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: But there are also other schemes that are focused on bringing in technology, bringing in strategic investments, which we may or may not have the capability among the local industries.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Therefore, we will need to assess each project's features and background to see whether it is appropriate to incorporate local enterprise collaboration.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Instead of being able to attract these technology, experts, network and opportunities here, you may lose them because we do not have the local capability to support them.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: But where possible, we will always encourage MNCs investing here to work with our local enterprises.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Where possible, where appropriate, we will have the conversation with the grant applicants, to see whether local SMEs can play a part, and it is something that we always push for and encourage.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: In fact, many of the investors who come to Singapore are also looking at the capability of the SMEs, the local enterprises here.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: This is the whole ecosystem that we are developing.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: That is actually one of our key selling points, and very often, when I talk to investors, they choose Singapore, not just because of our grants, but because of the ecosystem that we have developed.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: They can tap on the SMEs capability to augment their business and that is why they are here.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: But at the same time, as I said, through PACT, we are hoping to level up the capability of SMEs, so that they, too, can continue to grow, as the MNCs are growing.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Where possible and applicable, we definitely will take into account collaboration with the local enterprises.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Chairman, I want to thank the Member, Ms Foo Mee Har, for her question.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: I think she notes that this is a MTI COS debate and I outlined the new schemes that Enterprise Singapore colleagues have launched, which is the Heartlands Placemaking Grant (HEPG).

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: And in her cut, I recall that she, and many other Members, spoke very passionately about the unique role of heartland enterprises in Singapore, and I completely agree with them.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: That is why we are always leaning forward, going the extra mile for our heartland enterprises, especially during the COVID-19 period.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: And I think, we can all agree that the heartland shops are literally close to our homes and also close to our hearts.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: First, they provide the convenience and also a wide assortment of products and services and, most of the time, daily necessities and essential products and services.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Second, they also provide jobs to a lot of our residents who do not want to travel too far for their day job, or maybe part-time job, but just want a job nearby.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: But very importantly, they inject vibrancy into all our neighbourhoods, the kampung spirit, the community spirit.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: And that is why in MTI and Enterprise Singapore, we are always going the extra mile to support our heartland shops in going digital, in embracing transformation and also reaching out to new customers, not just customers who cannot visit their shop physically, but also customers overseas, by going online or even adopting digital platforms.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: In the same vein, we are always looking out for like-minded partners within the whole-of-Government.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: So, frankly, if Members remember how CDC Vouchers came about, it came about because of the circuit breaker.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Coming out of the circuit breaker, we felt it was very important to support lower-income households.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: At the same time, our heartland shops had been closed for two months, and two months of closure can really make or break these heartland shops.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Back then, it was Deputy Prime Minister Heng who launched the $20 million paper voucher, because our sense back then was that the paper voucher will be more effective.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: And then six months later, in January 2021, another tranche of $20 million.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Prime Minister Lee Hsien Loong launched the first nationwide digital CDC Vouchers.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: We say digital, but we also gave assurance to residents who do not have smartphones, we assured them that they can print their CDC Vouchers in any of the Community Centres, to provide them the convenience.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: If Members remember, that was $100 for each of the 1.22 million households.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Then five months later, Deputy Prime Minister Lawrence Wong launched a second tranche.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: A few days ago, I just did a check on the numbers.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: And if we include the fourth tranche, which is ongoing, the amount that has been spent at our heartland shops and hawkers amount to $133 million.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: So, it means that the three tranches we have completed and the ongoing fourth tranche have catalysed spending of $540 million in our 23,000 heartland shops and hawkers.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: The key point is that it is not just MTI, it is not just Enterprise Singapore that is going the extra mile to support our heartland shops for them to innovate, for them to transform, for them to future-proof themselves in this digital era.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: We are also working with the Federation of Merchants' Associations, Singapore (FMAS), Heartland Enterprise Centre Singapore (HECS), and we welcome each and every one of you, wearing your different hats, to share with us how you would like to also synergise the efforts to support our heartland shops, because they are close to our homes and close to our hearts.

speaker: Mr Chairman
text: So, for those who want to seek clarifications, and likewise, for the responses, please keep them short.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: The first is for Minister of State Low.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: So, in terms of the so-called loophole for the lemon law whereby used cars that are sold on consignment are actually not covered, does the Government intend to plug this loophole, given that it is likely the largest value item for a given household?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: The second is more for Minister Dr Tan.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: I think the Minister mentioned the power plants that will be coming up will be hydrogen-ready.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: So, I just wanted to understand, in terms of the feedstock that they will be using when they are operational, is there a target percentage for them to be using hydrogen?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: And similar as to how we deal with LNG, does the Government intend to do a kind of centralised procurement of, say, ammonia or hydrogen feedstock for economies of scale?

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Chairman, I promise to keep it short so that you can enjoy your peach oolong tea.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: When the Member talked about lemon law, is he talking about owner selling to owner or business selling to owner?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: Basically, the used car dealers, when they actually sell on behalf of the owner to somebody buying a second-hand car.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Okay, I want to thank the Member for the clarification.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: The used cars that are sold by car dealers on behalf of the owners, they are also known as consignment cars.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: They are really considered consumer-to-consumer (C2C) transactions between the owner and the buyer.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: So, if the Member knows of any, please let us know and we will follow up.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: We also want to use this platform to really advise the consumers to take extra precaution when making such purchases.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, today, this is the new breed of CCGTs that, if there is any planting and so on, we envisage that they should make that transition pathway.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: To the Member's point in terms of hydrogen, today, in countries particularly where they have a favourable geographical advantage, where they have solar power or wind or tidal, they can produce green hydrogen.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The logistics and transportation of the hydrogen is very, very costly today because the boiling point of liquid hydrogen is very, very low.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: A significant amount of energy is needed to keep it at that kind of low temperatures.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, it does not make it economically viable.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Having said that, we are not resting on our laurels.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Hence, we have the ammonia pathfinder project, where we started to see how, on a very small scale, we can conduct a pilot.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We are also working through our initiatives to see, in terms of the supply chains, what kind of technological advancements and developments we can go further in, to make the transportation of hydrogen a lot more cost effective.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: In terms of central procurement, obviously, at a point in time, when we have arrived at that technological maturity, we can certainly consider that.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: But at this particular point in time, even if you have nuclear power, to use it to do the electrolysis of water to produce hydrogen, it is still not green hydrogen.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, that is a technical specification that is needed.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant
text: I want to thank Minister of State Alvin Tan for answering so many questions on tourism and internationalisation, and for the $300 million boost to the Tourism Development Fund.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant
text: My question for you is, which schemes have worked well for Tourism Development Fund.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant
text: On a different point, what strategies were involved in bringing Taylor Swift to Singapore, which in my view has been very successful in terms of a branding on an international stature?

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: And actually, next week, there are a couple of Parliamentary Questions and that will be very tailored towards this particular question in detail.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: All of these different aspects that we have put in, I wanted to remind Members that our tourism sector was really, really hard hit during COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: So, in 2022, we pumped in $500 million for the Tourism Development Fund.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: That helped significantly to prepare our very, very hard-hit tourism sector to recover.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Now, they have recovered, as I mentioned in my main reply, and this $300 million top-up will also continue to boost them so that we can attract both very high-quality lifestyle entertainment acts as well as top world-class MICE events to Singapore, and just to lift Singapore to be in a very attractive lifestyle and as well as a business destination.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Our current guillotine time is 4.15 pm, but it included a 20-minute break.

speaker: The Chairman
text: So, if Members do not mind, we will have a very, very short break.

speaker: The Chairman
text: I will allow more clarifications, if Members do not mind, but it will eat into our break time.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: I have a couple of clarifications for Minister Gan.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: I think I heard Minister Gan mention earlier about precision medicine.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: So, I just wanted to ask for a bit more details about the Ministry's assessment of what sort of potential that precision medicine can have as a growth area in relation to the Singapore economy.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: The second point relates to whether MTI is currently working with agencies like the Ministry of Health (MOH) and the Health Promotion Board (HPB) in relation to addressing some of the concerns around precision medicine, because at the moment, it is quite prohibitively expensive.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: I am just concerned about accessibility to those who might not have a high income.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: So, whether they can share details about the work that is being done with MOH or HPB in relation to addressing some of these concerns.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: I have given a broad perspective of the potential for the precision medicine market in my speech.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: I think you can refer to that in terms of the numbers.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: But in terms of the specific areas of potential, this is a very early stage of an emerging technology.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: As some Members have said, if we do not move in time, we will never have time to move.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: So, I think it is something for which we have to grab the opportunity to work with companies who are in this field to develop new technologies.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: The potential is to find new solutions and new therapies by working on genomics and see how the genes interact with one another; and also coupled with the advent of AI that has made precision medicine even more promising.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: So, this is an area that we are well positioned to collaborate with leaders in the world to develop this particular sector.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean
text: The question is to Minister of State Alvin Tan.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean
text: I think we are very cheered by the positive news on tourism.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean
text: I just wanted to make a point that we do have a number of people coming up from our universities and our schools who are very talented in terms of being creative professionals.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean
text: I think many of them would desire the opportunity to be on the stage together with many of these different acts coming into Singapore.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean
text: So, my pitch to MTI is whether we can then work very closely with the different, other agencies that are supporting the creatives, supporting the young people to give them the opportunities to come on board some of these programmes, some of these acts that come into Singapore to have the opportunity to build up their portfolio.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: In the tourism sector, we have a variety of programmes that, through the Tourism Development Fund that I mentioned earlier on, it is not just infrastructure and bringing in these acts and MICE events, but it is also helping to build our tourism sector.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: I have launched very countless scholarships that we work together with the institute of higher learning (IHLs), polytechnics, the Institute of Technical Education (ITE) and others, to help to boost up that pool of talent.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Just wearing my MCCY hat, I will explain a little bit more.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The SG Arts Plan has a very, very strong focus on all of these different talents; not just in place-making, which Minister Edwin Tong mentioned earlier on, but also to enhance our artists' capability in many of these, so that we equip them as we bring all of these acts and all of these events into Singapore, they have a good chance to be able to participate in them.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee
text: Chairman, I thank Minister Gan for his insightful response to hon Member Ms Foo Mee Har.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee
text: I just want to press on and maybe have further clarification to her question about nurturing our local SMEs.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee
text: I think many businesses, including ours, when we expand our international operations and doing coveted project bids where the local Government has provided tax incentives and other incentives to the client, they actually have a clear policy and practice for us to require local partnerships, even with partners that have very limited or no existing capabilities.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee
text: I guess such policies are aimed to foster local participation and skills transfer.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee
text: I am wondering if MTI can consider doing some research on this and see what the trade-offs are if we enforce such collaboration.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee
text: I think my second clarification is to Minister of State Low in regard to the EEG.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee
text: I was wondering if MTI can allow or consider whether some of the EEG-approved equipment to be used across all industries.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee
text: For example, the electric forklift is almost double the price of a diesel forklift and these are all applicable to almost all industries.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: In the interest of the bubble tea, I will keep it short.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We need to balance the trade-offs and sometimes, you have to look at the potential investment.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: If the investment is strategic to us, it is very important for us to bring in markets, to bring in technology and to bring in opportunities.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Eventually, this will spill over to local industries.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Rather than to have a very hard-wired requirement that all of them must have a local partnership.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: You will find that you may, in the end, lose out more opportunities than gain the opportunities.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: At the same time, we also provide schemes and support for the local industries to level them up, so that they are able to then work together with these large enterprises to add value to them.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: At the end of the day, economics must make sense for both parties.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Government grants and schemes are just to facilitate and to push them, to nudge them to come together.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: But in the end, when the two of them want to get married, the marriage must make sense.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We are the matchmaker and we try to facilitate and give a little bit of encouragement here and there, but at the end, the economics must work out together for both of them.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: I want to thank Mr Mark Lee for his request and question.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: I want to assure him that we certainly will help our SMEs to invest in energy-efficient equipment.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: As I mentioned, when we launched this two years ago, the sectors that we approved are food manufacturing, food services and retail.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Because when you look at their operating expenditure, electricity was a key component.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: I must say, it is capped at $30,000.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: I want to assure him that we will continue to work with other champion agencies outside MTI to also understand what the other industries and sectors that will benefit from it.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: The EEG will be open to other industries such as maritime, construction and data centres by the end of this year.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: I welcome SBF and TACs to work with us, to be a voice for the sectors and bridge the conversation with MTI and our economic agency on this front.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Like many of you, I am also thirsty and a little bit hungry.

text: So, Mr Liang, would you like to withdraw your amendment?

text: And I am sure Minister Tan See Leng's personal charm must have made a difference there.

text: With that, I also want to thank Minister Gan, Minister Tan, Minister of State Low Yen Ling and Minister of State Alvin Tan for their comprehensive replies to our responses.

text: I propose to take a short break now.
